explanation: weird is labelled fear 43 times and surprise 34 times in the training split. The context (an awkward conversation about another person) fits either reading, so neither label can be derived from the text: the gold label is effectively a coin flip between the two classes the annotation assigns to this word.

Three words. stressed is labelled sadness 53 times and anger 37 times in training, and there is no context to disambiguate. Emphatic do adds intensity, not a direction. The best possible strategy is to guess the majority label, which is what TF-IDF + LR does; BERT and the BiLSTM guess the minority label.

blessed is labelled joy 45 times and love 38 times. Gratitude towards readers ('share it with you all') lies on the boundary between the two classes; the label set does not say where gratitude belongs, and the annotation treats it inconsistently.

phenomenon: Split keyword; target of the emotion
explanation: agitated is divided between fear (41) and anger (39) in training. The prepositional phrase with myself names the target of the emotion, and self-blame for not foreseeing a break-up is anger directed at oneself. The models' anger is linguistically better motivated than the gold fear.

phenomenon: Label assigned from a lexicon word, not from the stated emotion
explanation: The emotion is stated explicitly (i feel very cheated), and cheated is a negative word (sadness 4, anger 4 in training). The gold label joy cannot come from it; it matches supporting (joy 48 / love 46 in training) later in the sentence. Occlusion confirms that BERT also relies on supporting. This is direct evidence that labels were assigned from an emotion word in the text rather than from the meaning of the sentence.

The sentence ends with 'a magical world of love', and kissing and sweet lips describe romantic affection. The gold joy is supported only by paradise. BERT's love is the more plausible reading: for romantic happiness the two classes overlap.

These are song lyrics ('the walls just disappeared ... im unprotected'). Test text 591 is the same lyric with almost identical wording but is labelled sadness; this one is labelled fear. The same input carries two gold labels, so any classifier must miss at least one of them.

There is no emotion in the sentence: cold refers to temperature and the text praises a fabric. In training, 'feel cold' is labelled anger in all 22 texts, so the annotation maps the word cold to anger regardless of its sense. The BiLSTM has learned this convention (anger); BERT and LR follow the positive evaluation 'the fabric is great' (joy).

phenomenon: Rare word split into misleading subwords
explanation: angsty occurs in only 2 training texts. BERT's WordPiece tokenizer splits it into ang + ##sty; deleting angsty lowers P(anger) by 0.99 (occlusion), so the anger prediction comes from this word, plausibly through the piece ang shared with angry. Without it BERT predicts sadness from listless, a reliable sadness keyword (45 of 45 training texts), which the word-level models follow.

phenomenon: Scraping residue and an inconsistent label
explanation: After 'i feel unprotected' the text continues with HTML residue (a class post count link href http). unprotected occurs in 3 training texts, all labelled fear, so BERT, the BiLSTM and TF-IDF + LR all predict fear with near certainty. The gold sadness conflicts with how the same word is labelled in training.

No emotion word: the writer reports failing a test for the second time. Recognising sadness requires appraisal knowledge (failure at a valued goal). flunked never occurs in training. Occlusion shows that BERT's joy rests mainly on bs; the BiLSTM is correct.

phenomenon: Implicit emotion in an event description
explanation: A situation is described without an emotion word, in the style of the 'when ...' event descriptions in the dataset. The anger arises from appraising other people's lack of skill as an obstacle; the surface vocabulary (playing, sport, advanced) is neutral or positive, so BERT, the BiLSTM and TF-IDF + LR all predict joy with high confidence.

phenomenon: Emotion word with a different experiencer
explanation: happy describes the other person ('make the person happy'), not the writer: the experiencer of the emotion word is not the speaker. Models that map emotion words to labels without identifying the experiencer predict joy (BERT 1.00). The gold anger cannot be recovered from this fragment alone.

phenomenon: Emotion of a third person in quoted speech
explanation: The sentence is a quotation attributed to a third person (said assessor steve helm). hated (anger 14 / sadness 10 in training) describes how other people feel about him, not the speaker's emotion. The text gives no basis for choosing between sadness and anger.

phenomenon: Competing emotion cues in a long text
explanation: The text contains cues of four classes: feeling for him (sympathy), awful predicament (sadness), so glad (joy) and disgusted (anger). The annotator chose sadness, BERT joy with 0.51 confidence (almost a tie). A single-label scheme forces one emotion where the discourse expresses a sequence of emotions.

The writer reports the absence of joy (did not feel any passionate joy), yet the gold label is joy: in training, texts with a negated emotion word almost always carry that word's label (§4.3). BERT predicts love from passionate (joy 35 / love 48). Neither the annotation nor the model takes the scope of not into account.

The house 'remained at a balmy' (the temperature that followed has been cut off) after the writer felt like 'suffering from hypothermia': balmy is ironic. Occlusion shows that BERT's joy depends on balmy (drop 0.66); the word-level models follow suffering and are correct.

phenomenon: Mock-solemn hyperbole with an unsupported label
explanation: 'The depth of sorrow' is a humorous exaggeration about not having posted 'ludicrous rants'. BERT and TF-IDF + LR read sorrow literally (sadness, BERT 0.99); the BiLSTM predicts surprise. The gold surprise is not supported by any emotion word in the text (ludicrous is labelled sadness 6 times and surprise 3 times in training).
